The school hall was packed for Monday assembly, and Ritu's hands were damp around her three index cards. Her topic: why the school should start a recycling drive.
Backstage, Afreen squeezed her arm. "Remember the plan. Story, three points, one ask."
Ritu walked to the mic. Four hundred faces. Her mind went blank for a second. She looked at the first card: "The bin behind the canteen."
"Last week," she began, "I counted forty plastic bottles in one bin behind our canteen."
A few students looked up. Her voice steadied. She made her three points, pausing after each, and ended: "Bring one bottle to the green box on Friday."
Afreen was clapping hardest. On Friday, the green box was overflowing.

Dear Lalremsiami didi,
You asked how my first district-level speech went. Honestly? My knees were shaking so hard I thought the audience could see.
I used your trick. I didn't memorise every word. Just the opening line, three key points on a card, and the closing line. When I forgot what came next, I looked at the card, took a breath, and carried on.
The best part was the story about my grandfather's village well. The hall went quiet. I could feel them listening.
I came third. My friends said I sounded calm. I didn't feel calm! But now I know that fear doesn't show as much as I thought.
Thank you for making me practise in front of the mirror.
Chinmay

qa.a: Chinmay felt very nervous and afraid the audience could see the fear.

Uday, you asked about my first big speech, so here it is. I'm Tarun, and I used to be the kid who'd pretend to be sick on presentation days.
Class 11, I had to give a talk at the science fair opening. Two hundred people. I wrote the whole thing out, word for word, and on the morning I couldn't remember line one.
My teacher said, "Forget the script. What's the one thing you want them to remember?" I said, "That the river near our school is dying." She said, "Start there."
So I did. I started with a photo of the river. I told them what I'd seen, then what we could do. I didn't read anything.
My voice shook for the first minute. Then people started nodding, and I forgot to be scared. That's when I learnt: people don't need you perfect. They need you clear.

qa.a: Two hundred people.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling on the morning he couldn't remember line one?
qa.a: Tarun felt panicked and anxious, with the fully written script failing him.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned Tarun's speech around?
qa.a: Dropping the script and starting from the one thing Tarun wanted people to remember, the dying river, with a photo.

qa.q: How might Tarun's teacher have seen the speech?
qa.a: The teacher probably felt proud, seeing Tarun connect with the audience once the talk came from what Tarun cared about.

It was 1 a.m. in Seoul, and Soo-ah was still watching short videos. She'd opened the app "for five minutes" after dinner.
Every video ended and the next one started by itself. Dance clips, then a cat, then a makeup video, then more dance clips. She kept thinking, "Just one more."
The next morning, her friend Clara showed her the app's settings. "See? It learns what you watch longest and shows more of that. And autoplay is on by default. It's designed so you don't stop."
Soo-ah felt strange, like she'd been tricked. That night she turned off autoplay and set a timer. When the video ended, the screen just stopped.
She sat in the quiet for a second, then put the phone on her desk and went to sleep.

qa.a: Soo-ah felt uneasy and a bit tricked, realising the app was designed to keep her watching.

In the school's computer club, Ramesh Sir put a question on the board: "Why is the like button red?"
Deepika laughed. "Because it's pretty?"
"Red grabs attention. The number of likes makes you check again. Notifications come at random times, like a slot machine. The feed never ends, so there's no natural stop."
Deepika thought about how she'd checked her post's likes eleven times yesterday.
"So the app wants me to keep looking?"
"The company earns more when you stay longer. That doesn't make you weak. It just means you're up against a design."
That evening, Deepika turned off like-count notifications. She still posted. But she didn't check eleven times.

Dear Anjali,
You asked why I deleted the video app. Here's why.
Last month I noticed something. I'd open it to watch one football clip. Then an hour would vanish. The app knew I liked football, so it kept showing football, then fights, then weird angry videos I didn't even like, but I kept watching because they made me feel something.
I read that these apps measure how long you stay and push whatever keeps you there. Not what's good for you. Just what keeps you.
I'm not saying you have to delete it. But try this: before you open it, decide what you're there for. When you've seen it, close it. And turn off notifications.
I've got my evenings back. I've started drawing again.
Your big brother,
Nilesh

qa.a: Nilesh felt uneasy and frustrated that the app took so much time with videos he didn't even like.

"This is hilarious," said Leela. "I'm posting it."

In the Kolkata school library, Sharmila watched Disha paste AI answers into her biology worksheet.
"Aren't you going to read it?"
"Why? It's right."
Sharmila pointed at one line. "It says plants take in oxygen for photosynthesis. That's backwards."
Disha frowned. "Oh."
"The tool is good for explaining, but you have to check. And if you just copy, you won't know it in the exam."
Disha sighed. "Okay. What do you do?"
"I ask it to explain a topic like I'm twelve. Then I close it, and write the answer myself. Then I check with the book."
Disha tried it. It took longer. But afterwards she could explain photosynthesis without looking.

qa.q: What did the AI get backwards?
qa.a: That plants take in oxygen for photosynthesis.

qa.a: Disha felt a bit reluctant and frustrated that checking would take longer.

qa.a: It uses AI to understand, but Disha writes and checks the answer herself, so she learns and catches errors.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel when Disha can explain photosynthesis without looking?
qa.a: Sharmila probably feels pleased that her approach helped Disha actually learn.

I'm Kashish, Gurpreet's younger sibling. Last Saturday, Gurpreet wanted to go to a friend's birthday party that ended at eleven. Papa's rule is home by nine.
I expected a fight. Instead, Gurpreet sat down at dinner and said, "Can I explain first?"
Papa nodded, arms crossed.
"It's at Simar's house, three streets away. Her parents will be there. I'll share my location, and I'll call at nine. If you want, you can pick me up at eleven."
Papa looked at Mummy. Mummy said, "You've been coming home on time all month."
Papa said, "Ten thirty. And I pick you up."
Gurpreet said, "Deal." I couldn't tell if Gurpreet was happy or just relieved. But nobody shouted.

qa.a: Gurpreet was probably nervous but hopeful, wanting to be heard without a fight.

qa.a: Gurpreet gave clear details, offered safety steps like sharing location and a call, and had a month of coming home on time.

qa.a: Kashish expected a fight and is surprised that it ended in a calm agreement.

Sarita beta, you're arguing with your father about going to Pune for college. Let me tell you about me and my father.
I was seventeen. I wanted to study engineering in Bombay. My father wanted me to stay and run his cloth shop. We shouted. I slammed doors.
Then my mother said, "Shouting won't work. Show him you've thought about it."
So I wrote down everything: the college, the fees, where I'd stay, how I'd come home every Diwali, and how I'd help with the shop accounts by post. I gave it to him.
He read it for three days. Then he said, "Go. But write to your mother every week."
I did. Your Rafiq dada learnt that respect works better than shouting.

In the kasba, everyone compared Rukmini with her cousin Shalini. Shalini always came first. Rukmini came somewhere in the middle.
At the family dinner after results, her uncle said, "Shalini got 96. Rukmini, what happened?"
Rukmini stared at her plate. Her ears burned.
Shalini put down her spoon. "Rukmini made the best science model in the district. She did that alone."
Everyone went quiet.
Later, on the terrace, Rukmini said, "Thanks. But I still feel like the second one."
Shalini shrugged. "I'm scared all the time of not coming first. It's not fun either."
They sat in silence. Rukmini realised: nobody at the top was feeling great either.

In Warsaw, the school posted everyone's rank online. Marek was 27th out of 30. His phone buzzed with messages: "How'd you do?"
He didn't answer. At home, he lay on his bed and stared at the ceiling.
Bao, his friend, came over with a bag of chips. "I saw. I'm 19th. Want to be sad together?"
Marek laughed despite himself. "My mum will be so disappointed."
"Did you try?"
"Yes. Maths was a disaster."
"Then that's the problem to fix. Not you."
They opened his maths paper. Bao pointed at three mistakes. "Same kind. You can learn this."
That evening, Marek told his mum, "I'll ask for extra help in maths." She hugged him.

qa.a: 27th out of 30.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling as he stared at the ceiling?
qa.a: Marek felt ashamed and dreaded his mum's disappointment.

qa.a: Bao separated the problem from Marek himself and helped him spot a pattern in his mistakes.

qa.a: His mum probably feels relieved and proud that he has a plan, which is why she hugs him.
